Urgent Problem and Differential

Sudden NLP with RAPD ten minutes post-IOL exchange demands urgent differentiation between anterior ischaemic optic neuropathy, posterior ischaemic optic neuropathy, and retrobulbar or intracranial pathology. The clear cornea, low IOP, and attached perfused retina exclude acute angle closure, suprachoroidal haemorrhage, and central retinal artery occlusion at the disc head. However, a normal fundus appearance does not exclude posterior ischaemic optic neuropathy, optic neuritis, or compressive lesions distal to the globe, as these produce no immediate visible disc change.

The prior vitrectomy and capsulotomy alter vitreous dynamics and may have permitted intracameral agents to reach the posterior segment, raising the possibility of direct optic nerve or retinal toxicity from phenylephrine or preservatives. This remains a hypothesis; the temporal proximity to injection is suggestive but not confirmatory.

Next Priorities

Urgent neuroimaging with contrast is essential to exclude compressive or demyelinating pathology. Formal visual field testing of the fellow eye, colour vision, and serial disc assessment over 24–72 hours will help distinguish PION from retrobulbar causes. Fluorescein angiography, if available, may reveal delayed choroidal filling suggesting posterior ciliary compromise. The full medication record should be reviewed for concentration, volume, and any inadvertent posterior migration.
